Tractian raises $130M Series D at $1.4B valuation
by Araceli Dominguez
October 23, 2026
1 minute read
0
Shares
Brazilian AI startup Tractian raised $130M in a Series D round at a $1.4B valuation. The round was led by Sapphire Ventures and Catalyst , M&G’s growth equity division. N47 , General Catalyst , Bosch Ventures , 53 Stations , Monashees , Endeavor Catalyst , Norte Ventures , and Y Combinator also participated.
Founded in 2019 Tractian develops AI solutions to monitor industrial equipment, detect failures, and recommend maintenance actions.
Tractian plans to invest the funding in research and development over the next five years, focusing on physical AI, training large language models, and purchasing Nvidia processors.
Tractian generates nearly $100M in annualized revenue, with half coming from the US. Its technology operates in more than 2,000 facilities, including those of Coca-Cola, Whirlpool, Embraer, and Eli Lilly.

Mavria raises $130 million to mass-produce modular AI data centers
Photo: Brett Sayles / Pexels
The Houston-area startup, backed by Paradigm, AMP PBC and others, wants to build data centers in a factory instead of on site
by
Diego Almada Lopez
Mon 9 Nov 2026 · 13:12 EST
·
3 min read
In Technology
Share

Data centers have traditionally been built like custom homes: one site, one design, one long list of headaches. Mavria wants to build them more like cars coming off an assembly line.
The Houston-area startup has raised a total of $130 million to scale manufacturing of its factory-built data centers. That includes a $100 million round led by Paradigm, which puts the company at a post-money valuation of $1 billion .
Unicorn status on launch day
Mavria launched on November 9, 2026. It arrived with a billion-dollar price tag and a product already on the production floor.
Paradigm led the round, but it brought company. The backer list also includes AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Liquid 2 and Dream Ventures.
The founding trio comes from an unusual place for a hardware startup: the US Department of Energy. CEO Adam Blake, Seth Cohen and Nick Poradek all previously worked at the agency.
The company’s first product line is called Terrain. Each unit is a standardized 5 MW block that bundles power, cooling and IT infrastructure into a single package.

The blocks are designed for high-density artificial intelligence workloads. The first unit, Terrain 01, is currently in production in Houston. Mavria has not disclosed which customers will deploy Terrain or where the units will go.
Why build a data center in a factory
The pitch is about repeatability. Conventional data center construction is site-specific, which means every project gets designed and built more or less from scratch.

Mavria’s bet is that AI infrastructure should move toward an industrialized model. Design one block, perfect it, then build it over and over.
The company frames the approach as a way to speed up AI infrastructure rollout. That rollout is currently running into two stubborn walls: power constraints and construction constraints.
Standardized blocks attack the construction problem directly. If most of the work happens on a factory floor, less of it has to happen on a muddy job site.
The 5 MW unit size also matters. Modular blocks theoretically let an operator add capacity in increments rather than committing to a single giant build all at once.
The investor lineup tells its own story
A $100 million lead check is a strong signal at any stage. The supporting cast adds weight too. AMP PBC, Critical Frontier, Liquid 2 and Dream Ventures all joined Paradigm on the cap table.
Still, a $1 billion valuation before any disclosed customer deployment sets a high bar. Investors are pricing in the factory’s future output, not its current one.

Clay raises $115M in Series D funding round at $7.1B valuation
SaasRise • Oct 2, 2026
Type Venture Funding - Series D
Value $115M
Clay Company
Clay, the AI‑powered GTM infrastructure startup, closed a $115 million Series D round in September 2026, lifting its post‑money valuation to $7.1 billion. The financing follows a rapid growth trajectory that saw ARR triple to $100 million and an employee tender offer at a $5 billion valuation. The new capital will fund product expansion, the emerging GTM‑engineer role, and broader market adoption.
Clay announced a $115 million Series D financing on September 2026 that values the company at $7.1 billion, marking the latest milestone in its AI‑driven go‑to‑market platform rollout. The round, whose investors were not disclosed, comes on the heels of a February report that Clay had tripled its annual recurring revenue to $100 million in a single year and a prior employee tender offer that pegged the firm at a $5 billion valuation.
Deal Terms
The Series D injects $115 million of growth capital into Clay’s product and engineering teams. While the lead investor was not named, the financing round is positioned to accelerate the development of Claygent—Clay’s OpenAI‑powered agent that automates research, data enrichment, and outreach across sales, marketing, and recruiting. The company also unveiled a $1 million scholarship fund to train the nascent GTM‑engineer profession, underscoring its commitment to building an ecosystem around its platform.
Market Context
Since its 2017 launch in Brooklyn, Clay has evolved from a no‑code spreadsheet tool into a full‑stack GTM infrastructure layer. By embedding AI across the revenue stack, it enables teams to replace manual, multi‑tool workflows with repeatable, agentic systems. The rapid ARR growth and soaring valuation reflect a broader market shift toward AI‑augmented revenue operations, where investors are rewarding platforms that can both generate expansion revenue and create new job categories—evidenced by the emerging GTM‑engineer role that Clay coined in 2023.
The Series D capital will fund product enhancements, deeper integrations with data sources, and expansion into adjacent verticals where AI‑driven revenue automation is still nascent. With more than 10,000 founders, investors, and operators gathering at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Clay is poised to showcase its roadmap and capture additional enterprise customers looking to scale growth without proportionally expanding headcount.
Why It Matters
Clay’s infusion of $115 million gives it the runway to outpace rivals such as Cursor, Lovable, and Webflow, which are also courting the GTM‑engineer talent pool. By formalizing a scholarship program and branding the role, Clay can lock in early adopters and create a network effect that makes its platform the default stack for AI‑native revenue teams. Competitors will need to accelerate their own AI integrations or risk losing market share to a solution that already bundles data access, workflow automation, and an OpenAI‑backed research agent.
For operators, the deal signals that building an internal GTM‑engineering capability may no longer be a cost center but a strategic differentiator. articles.title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
articles.snippet: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation TechCrunch
articles.text:
Technology
October 20, 2026 / TechCrunch News / 0 Comments
SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.
The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.
“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.
And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.
Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.
Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.
The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.
Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.
“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.
The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)
While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.
